topics: A. Mendelian Genetics and Basic Concepts
E. Cell Cycle, Mitosis and Meiosis

subjective.topic: A. Mendelian Genetics and Basic Concepts
subjective.question: Write the sub-types (sub-disciplines) of genetics.
subjective.answer: There are four sub-disciplines of genetics, although some geneticists classify genetics into many sub-disciplines: (1) Transmission (Classical) Genetics, (2) Population Genetics, (3) Quantitative Genetics, (4) Molecular Genetics.

subjective.topic: A. Mendelian Genetics and Basic Concepts
subjective.question: Write the modern genetics concepts.
subjective.answer: Modern genetics concepts include: chromosomes and gene(s); Mendelian genetics and non-Mendelian genetics; genotypes and phenotypes; mutations and polymorphism.

subjective.topic: A. Mendelian Genetics and Basic Concepts
subjective.question: What is a gene?
subjective.answer: A gene is a heredity unit on chromosomes.

subjective.topic: A. Mendelian Genetics and Basic Concepts
subjective.question: What is a trait?
subjective.answer: A trait is the variation for a character (i.e. brown, black, white etc.).

subjective.topic: A. Mendelian Genetics and Basic Concepts
subjective.question: Define allele.
subjective.answer: An allele is one of the possible forms of a gene. Most genes have two alleles, a dominant allele and a recessive allele. If an organism is heterozygous for that trait, or possesses one of each allele, then the dominant trait is expressed. Alleles were first defined by Gregor Mendel in the law of segregation.

subjective.topic: A. Mendelian Genetics and Basic Concepts
subjective.question: Define genotype and phenotype.
subjective.answer: Genotype and phenotype: the genetic make-up of an organism is called genotype, while the physical appearance of an organism is called phenotype.

subjective.topic: A. Mendelian Genetics and Basic Concepts
subjective.question: Define dominant and recessive traits.
subjective.answer: A dominant trait is one that is phenotypically expressed in heterozygotes. A recessive trait is expressed only when two copies of the gene are present. In Mendel's experiments, the trait that expressed itself over the other (e.g. round over wrinkled) was dominant, while the trait that did not show in the first generation (wrinkled) was recessive.

subjective.topic: A. Mendelian Genetics and Basic Concepts
subjective.question: Define locus.
subjective.answer: A locus (plural loci) in genetics is a fixed position on a chromosome, like the position of a gene or a marker (genetic marker). Each chromosome carries many genes; humans have an estimated 19,000-20,000 haploid protein-coding genes on the 23 different chromosomes.

subjective.topic: A. Mendelian Genetics and Basic Concepts
subjective.question: Why did Mendel choose the garden pea for his experiments? Write the properties of the garden pea.
subjective.answer: Mendel used pea plants because they can either self-pollinate or be cross-pollinated, and they have a very short life cycle. Properties of the garden pea: it is easy to cultivate and grew well in his garden; its flowers are hermaphrodite, i.e. the pea plant has both male and female sexual organs; it has a short generation time; it produces many offspring; and its seeds occur in a variety of shapes and colours.

subjective.topic: A. Mendelian Genetics and Basic Concepts
subjective.question: How did Mendel prove heredity in variation among individuals?
subjective.answer: He deduced that genes come in pairs and are inherited as distinct units, one from each parent. Mendel tracked the segregation of parental genes and their appearance in the offspring as dominant or recessive traits. He recognized the mathematical patterns of inheritance from one generation to the next.

subjective.topic: A. Mendelian Genetics and Basic Concepts
subjective.question: What are the expectations of Mendel's law of inheritance?
subjective.answer: Gregor Mendel crossed various pure lines of garden peas and, by following their hybrid progeny, observed that traits are inherited as alternate states of independent units of inheritance or genes (which Mendel called "factors"), and that these units come in pairs.

subjective.topic: A. Mendelian Genetics and Basic Concepts
subjective.question: State the law of independent assortment with an example.
subjective.answer: Alleles for different traits are distributed to sex cells independently of one another; traits are transmitted to offspring independently of one another. Example: a dihybrid cross of true-breeding plants for two traits - a plant with green pod colour and yellow seed colour (GGYY, both dominant) cross-pollinated with a plant having yellow pod colour and green seeds (ggyy, both recessive) gives F1 plants that are heterozygous GgYy.

subjective.topic: A. Mendelian Genetics and Basic Concepts
subjective.question: Define the chromosomal theory of inheritance.
subjective.answer: The chromosomal theory of inheritance states that genes have specific loci on chromosomes. Mendel proposed the law of segregation and the law of independent assortment to explain the inheritance behind his pea plant traits; later, Boveri and Sutton developed the chromosome theory of inheritance, which stated that chromosomes were responsible for the heredity Mendel observed.

subjective.topic: A. Mendelian Genetics and Basic Concepts
subjective.question: Differentiate between particulate and blending inheritance.
subjective.answer: The particulate hypothesis was offered by Gregor Mendel, who discovered that traits are inherited in discrete units that we now know as genes. Instead of blending, the offspring inherits a version of a gene, called an allele, from each of the parents. Only one allele is expressed depending on a number of factors. (Blending inheritance, by contrast, held that parental traits blend in the offspring.)

subjective.topic: A. Mendelian Genetics and Basic Concepts
subjective.question: Differentiate between monohybrid and dihybrid cross.
subjective.answer: Monohybrid cross: cross-fertilization of true-breeding plants which differ in just one character is called a monohybrid cross; with it, Mendel determined the segregation of alleles at a single gene locus. Dihybrid cross: determines whether alleles at two different gene loci segregate dependently or independently.

subjective.topic: A. Mendelian Genetics and Basic Concepts
subjective.question: Define pure cross and hybrid cross.
subjective.answer: Pure cross: a cross between a true-breed plant/animal with another true-breed plant/animal is called a pure cross. Hybrid cross: an organism that is the offspring of genetically dissimilar parents; in other words, offspring produced by breeding in plants or animals of dissimilar parents.

subjective.topic: A. Mendelian Genetics and Basic Concepts
subjective.question: Differentiate between Mendelian and non-Mendelian genetics.
subjective.answer: In Mendelian inheritance, each parent contributes one of two possible alleles for a trait. Non-Mendelian genetics covers patterns of inheritance that deviate from a Mendelian pattern, e.g. linkage, maternal effect, epigenetic inheritance and mitochondrial inheritance.

subjective.question: What are the types of variation?
subjective.answer: There are two types of variation: (1) Discontinuous variation - entirely genetically controlled, cannot be altered by external conditions (e.g. blood group, colour blindness, dwarfism). (2) Continuous variation - the situation in which there are many intermediates between the extremes (e.g. shade of hair colour between black and blond).

subjective.question: Differentiate between continuous and discontinuous variation.
subjective.answer: Variation is all the differences which exist between members of the same species. Continuous variation is variation that has no limit on the value that can occur within a population (many intermediates between extremes). Discontinuous variation is entirely genetically controlled, cannot be altered by external conditions, and falls into distinct categories (e.g. blood group, colour blindness, dwarfism).

subjective.question: Differentiate between acquired and inherited variations.
subjective.answer: Inherited variation: variation in a characteristic that is a result of genetic inheritance from the parents. Children usually look a little like their father and a little like their mother, but will not be identical to either parent; inherited variations result from the activity of genes, are genetically controlled and cannot be altered (e.g. blood groups, finger prints, sex). Acquired variation: a non-heritable change in a function or structure of a living organism caused after birth by disease, injury, accident, deliberate modification, repeated use, disuse, misuse, nutrition or other environmental influences during a lifetime.

subjective.question: Define co-dominance with examples.
subjective.answer: Co-dominance is a situation when both alleles appear in the phenotype; neither allele is dominant and both alleles are expressed in a heterozygous individual (parallel behaviour of both alleles). Examples: AB blood group (both A and B alleles equally expressed), roan fur in cattle (white and red hair equally expressed), roan inheritance and Appaloosa horse.

subjective.question: Define incomplete dominance.
subjective.answer: Incomplete dominance is a situation in which neither allele is dominant. A new phenotype appears which is a blend of both alleles.

subjective.question: Define multiple alleles with an example.
subjective.answer: Multiple alleles are three or more alternative forms of a gene (alleles) that can occupy the same locus. However, only two of the alleles can be present in a single organism. Example: the ABO system of blood groups is controlled by three alleles, only two of which are present in an individual.

subjective.question: Define mono-allelic, di-allelic and poly-allelic genes.
subjective.answer: 30% of genes in humans are di-allelic - they exist in two forms. 70% are mono-allelic; they exist only in one form. Few are poly-allelic.

subjective.question: Define polygenic traits with an example.
subjective.answer: Most traits are not controlled by a single gene locus, but by the combined interaction of many gene loci. These traits are called polygenic traits. Examples: human height, eye colour and pigmentation.

subjective.question: Define pleiotropy.
subjective.answer: The ability of a gene to affect an organism in many ways is called pleiotropy. Pleiotropy refers to an allele which has more than one effect on the phenotype.

subjective.question: Define epistasis with an example.
subjective.answer: Epistasis is a phenomenon in which the effect of one gene is dependent on the presence of one or more modifier genes; it is a type of polygenic inheritance where alleles at one gene locus can hide or prevent expression of alleles at a second gene locus. Example: in dogs, a dominant allele B gives black coat and recessive b gives brown, but a second gene (e) controls eumelanin deposition in fur; dogs homozygous recessive at this locus (ee) will have yellow fur no matter which alleles are at the first locus.

subjective.question: What are the complications to inheritance patterns?
subjective.answer: Complications to inheritance patterns include: multiple genes - epistasis and polygenic traits; and genes and the environment - sex-influenced traits and incomplete penetrance.

subjective.question: Differentiate between low and full (high) penetrance.
subjective.answer: Low penetrance: an allele with low penetrance will only sometimes produce the symptom or trait with which it has been associated at a detectable level; in low penetrance it is difficult to distinguish environmental from genetic factors. Highly (fully) penetrant: if an allele is highly penetrant, the trait it produces will almost always be apparent in an individual carrying the allele.

subjective.question: Explain genetic data / properties of genetic data.
subjective.answer: Genetic information is personal, permanent and predictive; it is used for diagnostics and treatments, and predictive information allows planning. Its applications include screening (newborn, selected population, carriers) and pharmacogenetics (individualized medicine). A genetic database is one or more sets of genetic data (genes, gene products, variants, phenotypes) stored together with software to enable users to retrieve genetic data, add genetic data and extract information from the data.

subjective.question: What is a chromosome?
subjective.answer: Genetic material in cells is organized into chromosomes. Prokaryotes generally have one circular chromosome. Eukaryotes have linear chromosomes in their nuclei.

subjective.question: What are the components of a typical chromosome? (as given in the sources)
subjective.answer: In humans, each cell normally contains 23 pairs of chromosomes, for a total of 46. Twenty-two of these pairs, called autosomes, look the same in both males and females. The 23rd pair, the sex chromosomes, differ between males and females.

subjective.question: Write the types of chromosomes.
subjective.answer: There are two types of eukaryotic chromosomes: (1) Autosomes - paired chromosomes with the same length, shape, centromere location and genes; any chromosomes other than sex chromosomes are called autosomes. (2) Sex chromosomes - members of a pair of chromosomes that differ between males and females.

subjective.question: Name the types of chromosomes based on centromere position.
subjective.answer: On the basis of centromere position, chromosomes are of four types: (1) Metacentric - centromere in the middle, two equal arms. (2) Submetacentric - centromere slightly away from the centre, arms unequal. (3) Acrocentric - centromere near one end, one arm very short. (4) Telocentric - centromere at the very end of the chromosome.

subjective.question: Differentiate between chromosome and chromatin.
subjective.answer: DNA exists in chromatin form in the nucleus. The chromatin condenses to form chromosomes during cell division. The chromatin in the nucleus forms a "beads-on-a-string" structure or nucleosome; the "beads" are octamer histone proteins and the "string" is the double-stranded DNA. Chromosomes are the rod-shaped, filamentous bodies present in the nucleus and are the carriers of genes; they are not visible in the active nucleus due to high water content but can be seen during cell division, as chromatin fibres undergo folding, coiling and supercoiling so the chromosomes become progressively thicker and smaller.

subjective.question: Define chromatin. Differentiate between euchromatin and heterochromatin.
subjective.answer: The complexes between eukaryotic DNA and proteins are called chromatin. Chromatin is made up of DNA, protein and RNA. There are two forms of chromatin in the interphase nucleus: euchromatin and heterochromatin. Cytologically, heterochromatin stains more intensely than euchromatin; heterochromatin is the tightly packed form of chromatin, often found at the periphery of the nucleus.

subjective.question: By which method can euchromatin be changed into heterochromatin?
subjective.answer: Histone methylation, histone deacetylation and the corepressor complex.

subjective.question: What is a nucleosome? Write a note on the different kinds of histone proteins.
subjective.answer: A nucleosome is a structural unit of a eukaryotic chromosome, consisting of a length of DNA coiled around a core of histones. Five abundant histones are H1, H2A, H2B, H3 and H4. The core histones are H2A, H2B, H3 and H4, which associate with DNA to form the nucleosome, while H1 (and its homologue H5) are linker histones involved in higher-order structures of chromatin.

subjective.question: Differentiate between nucleosome and nucleotide.
subjective.answer: Nucleosome: a structural unit of a eukaryotic chromosome, consisting of a length of DNA coiled around a core of histones. Nucleotide: a compound consisting of a nucleoside linked to a phosphate group; nucleotides form the basic structural unit of nucleic acids such as DNA.

subjective.question: What is the chromosome scaffold?
subjective.answer: Scaffold: (1) In genetics, the chromosome structure consisting entirely of non-histone proteins remaining after all the DNA and histone proteins have been removed from a chromosome. (2) In genomic mapping, a series of contigs that are in the right order but not necessarily connected in one continuous stretch of sequence.

subjective.question: What is chromosome topology?
subjective.answer: Chromosome compaction is a necessary feature of all living cells including bacteria. It is intricately linked to chromosome topology and the selective pressures introduced by gene organization along the genome sequence. This is referred to as the "transverse" chromosome topology.

subjective.question: What are polytene chromosomes? Give an example.
subjective.answer: Polytene (giant) chromosomes are found in the salivary glands of some Diptera. These chromosomes are very long and thick, hence known as giant chromosomes. They were first discovered by Balbiani in 1881 in dipteran salivary glands and are thus also known as salivary gland chromosomes. They have thousands of DNA strands and provide a high level of function in certain tissues such as salivary glands; the best understood are those of Drosophila, Chironomus and Rhynchosciara flies. Giant chromosomes have also been discovered in suspensors of young embryos of many plants, but these do not show the bands so typical of salivary gland chromosomes.

subjective.question: Write the types of banding in chromosomes.
subjective.answer: Q banding: Q bands are the fluorescent bands observed after quinacrine mustard staining with UV light; the distal ends are not stained by this technique. R banding: the R bands (reverse) are those located in the zones that do not fluoresce with quinacrine mustard, i.e. they are between the Q bands. C banding: the C bands correspond to constitutive heterochromatin. G banding (Giemsa banding): a technique used in cytogenetics to produce a visible karyotype by staining condensed chromosomes; heterochromatic regions, which tend to be rich in adenine and thymine (AT-rich) DNA and relatively gene-poor, stain more darkly in G-banding.

subjective.question: Which chemicals are used in chromosome banding?
subjective.answer: Quinacrine mustard is used in Q banding (fluorescent bands are observed with UV light after this staining), and Giemsa stain is used in G banding to produce a visible karyotype by staining condensed chromosomes.

subjective.question: Define sister chromatids.
subjective.answer: A sister chromatid refers to the identical copies (chromatids) formed by the replication of a chromosome, with both copies joined together by a common centromere. In other words, a sister chromatid may also be said to be "one-half" of the duplicated chromosome.

subjective.question: Differentiate between chromosome and chromatid.
subjective.answer: A chromosome is made up of two chromatids which are joined by the centromere. The chromatids separate from each other during mitosis to form two new chromosomes. The DNA making up a chromosome is dispersed as chromatin.

subjective.question: What are telomeres?
subjective.answer: The two ends of a chromosome are known as telomeres. These are required for the replication and stability of the chromosomes. When telomeres are damaged or removed due to chromosome breakage, the ends can readily fuse or unite with broken ends of other chromosomes.

subjective.question: Define CEN DNA and write its sub-domains. What is the kinetochore?
subjective.answer: Within the centromere region are locations where spindle fibres attach, which consist of DNA as well as protein. The actual location where the attachment occurs is called the kinetochore and is composed of both DNA and protein. The DNA sequence within these regions is called CEN DNA; it is 120 base pairs long and consists of sub-domains CDE-I, CDE-II and CDE-III.

subjective.question: What is linker DNA?
subjective.answer: Linker DNA is the stretch of DNA between two nucleosomes in the chromatin fibre. It connects adjacent nucleosomes (the "string" between the "beads" in the beads-on-a-string structure) and is the region where the linker histone H1 binds, helping in the higher-order packing of chromatin.

subjective.question: Differentiate between diploid and haploid cells.
subjective.answer: Diploid cells are body (somatic) cells; they are called (2n) cells and contain two sets of chromosomes - examples: skin cells, brain cells, bone cells, blood cells; in humans there are ~220 types of somatic cells. Haploid cells are sex cells (gametes); they are (n) cells containing one set of chromosomes - sperms and ova are gametes produced in males and females respectively.

subjective.question: Differentiate between prokaryotic and eukaryotic chromosomes.
subjective.answer: In prokaryotes, the circular chromosome is contained in the cytoplasm in an area called the nucleoid; prokaryotes usually have only one chromosome, which bears little morphological resemblance to eukaryotic chromosomes, and it exists as a highly folded and coiled structure dispersed throughout the cell. In eukaryotes, all of the cell's chromosomes are stored inside a structure called the nucleus; each eukaryotic chromosome is composed of DNA coiled and condensed around nuclear proteins called histones, is condensed and visible during cell division, and at the beginning of mitosis consists of two threads (sister chromatids) joined by a centromere.

subjective.question: Differentiate between monocot and dicot chromosomes.
subjective.answer: In general, plants have longer chromosomes than animals, and species having a lesser chromosome number usually have long chromosomes. Dicots in general have a higher number of chromosomes than monocots. Chromosomes are longer in monocots than in dicots.

subjective.question: Write the number of chromosomes in gold fish, chicken and fruit fly.
subjective.answer: In gold fish the number of chromosomes is 94. In chicken the number of chromosomes is 78, and in fruit fly the number of chromosomes is 8.

subjective.question: Define nucleotide, nucleoside, purine and pyrimidine.
subjective.answer: A nucleoside consists of a pentose sugar and a nitrogenous base, but no phosphate group. A nucleotide consists of a pentose sugar, a nitrogenous base and one to three phosphate groups; nucleotides form the basic structural unit of nucleic acids such as DNA. Purines and pyrimidines are nitrogenous bases that make up the two different kinds of nucleotide bases in DNA and RNA: the two-carbon nitrogen ring bases (adenine and guanine) are purines, while the one-carbon nitrogen ring bases (thymine and cytosine) are pyrimidines.

subjective.question: Name the three bonding parts which make a complete nucleotide.
subjective.answer: A nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar, and a phosphate.

subjective.question: Define the G-C rule and the cluster rule.
subjective.answer: G-C rule: the (G+C)% is constant within a species, but often differs between species. Cluster rule: pyrimidines often occur in clusters, and hence on the complementary strand purines do likewise. (These are among Chargaff's rules on DNA base composition; the GC rule and cluster rule reveal multiple levels of information in our genomes.)

subjective.question: Write a note on leading strand, lagging strand, Okazaki fragments and gyrase.
subjective.answer: Leading strand and lagging strand: when replication begins, the two parent DNA strands are separated; one strand of DNA is called the leading strand, which is replicated continuously in the 3' to 5' direction, while the other strand is called the lagging strand and is replicated discontinuously in short sections. Okazaki fragments: the small fragments formed during discontinuous replication of the lagging strand are called Okazaki fragments; during lagging strand synthesis, DNA ligase connects the Okazaki fragments after replacement of the RNA primers with DNA nucleotides. Gyrases: the double helical structure is opened by enzyme gyrase; these enzymes remove the helix (supercoiling) and produce a nick to uncoil DNA.

subjective.question: What are the major and minor grooves of DNA? (length and nucleotides in the major groove, as asked in past papers)
subjective.answer: The strand backbones are closer together on one side of the helix than on the other. The major groove occurs where the backbones are far apart; the minor groove occurs where they are close together. The grooves twist around the molecule on opposite sides. Certain proteins bind to DNA to alter its structure or to regulate transcription or replication. It is easier for these DNA-binding proteins to interact with the bases (the internal parts of the DNA molecule) on the major groove side because the backbones are not in the way. (The sources describe the grooves qualitatively and do not state numeric lengths.)

subjective.question: What was the work of Franklin and Wilkins?
subjective.answer: Genes are encoded in the sequence of bases, and the double helix model of DNA was supported by the work of Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins (their X-ray diffraction work on DNA fibres). The structure of DNA was discovered in 1953 by Francis Crick and James Watson.

subjective.question: What is the location of intronic sequences with respect to exons?
subjective.answer: Sequences that are joined together in the final mature RNA after RNA splicing are exons; introns are the intervening sequences located between exons within a gene. Introns are found in the genes of most organisms and many viruses, and can be located in a wide range of genes, including those that generate proteins, ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and transfer RNA (tRNA).

subjective.topic: E. Cell Cycle, Mitosis and Meiosis
subjective.question: What is interphase? Enlist the phases of the cell cycle.
subjective.answer: Interphase is the phase of the cell cycle in which a typical cell spends most of its life; during this phase the cell copies its DNA in preparation for mitosis, and it was formerly called the resting phase. Before a cell enters cell division it needs to take nutrients; preparation for division happens in three steps: G1 phase, S phase and G2 phase. The cell cycle has two main phases: (1) Interphase, (2) Mitotic phase (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase).

subjective.topic: E. Cell Cycle, Mitosis and Meiosis
subjective.question: Differentiate between G1, S phase and G2 phase.
subjective.answer: S phase: synthesis of new DNA for daughter cells. G1 phase: the new cell absorbs nutrients and grows larger. G2 phase: the cell continues to grow, gets too large and needs to divide.

subjective.topic: E. Cell Cycle, Mitosis and Meiosis
subjective.question: What is the mitotic apparatus?
subjective.answer: The spindle apparatus (or mitotic spindle) refers to the cytoskeletal structure of eukaryotic cells that forms during cell division to separate sister chromatids between daughter cells. Besides chromosomes, the spindle apparatus is composed of hundreds of proteins.

subjective.topic: E. Cell Cycle, Mitosis and Meiosis
subjective.question: Explain the prophase stage of mitosis.
subjective.answer: Prophase is the first phase of mitosis, the process that separates the duplicated genetic material carried in the nucleus of a parent cell into two identical daughter cells. Prophase is characterized by four events: (1) chromosomes condense and become more visible (DNA wraps around histones that condense it); (2) the nuclear membrane disappears; (3) centrioles are separated and take positions on the opposite poles of the cell; (4) spindle fibres form and radiate toward the centre of the cell.

subjective.topic: E. Cell Cycle, Mitosis and Meiosis
subjective.question: Write a note on prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase of mitosis.
subjective.answer: Prophase: chromosomes condense and become visible, the nuclear membrane disappears, centrioles separate to opposite poles and spindle fibres form. Metaphase: chromosomes line up across the middle of the cell; spindle fibres connect the centromere of each sister chromatid to the poles of the cell. Anaphase: the centromere splits, sister chromatids are separated and become individual chromosomes, and the separated chromatids move to opposite poles (securin destruction releases separase, resulting in split of centromeres); the cell stretches into an oval shape. Telophase: chromosomes start to uncoil, a nuclear envelope forms around the chromosomes at each pole, spindle fibres break down and dissolve, nucleoli reappear and a daughter nucleus is formed in each daughter cell - the effects of prophase are reversed.

subjective.topic: E. Cell Cycle, Mitosis and Meiosis
subjective.question: Define mitosis and meiosis.
subjective.answer: Cells give rise to new cells through a process called cell division. In mitosis, a cell divides once to produce two clones of itself, each with the same number of chromosomes. In meiosis, each cell divides twice, resulting in four daughter cells (gametes) that contain only half the number of chromosomes compared to the parent and are not necessarily identical.

subjective.topic: E. Cell Cycle, Mitosis and Meiosis
subjective.question: Differentiate between meiosis I and meiosis II.
subjective.answer: Meiosis I includes crossing over or recombination of genetic material between chromosome pairs, while meiosis II does not. Meiosis I has a long and complicated prophase I, split into five sub-phases. In meiosis II, the chromosomes are further separated into sister chromatids.

subjective.topic: E. Cell Cycle, Mitosis and Meiosis
subjective.question: What is the role of mitosis and meiosis in the animal body?
subjective.answer: There are two ways cell division can happen in humans and most other animals: mitosis and meiosis. When a cell divides by way of mitosis, it produces two clones of itself, each with the same number of chromosomes (growth and repair of the body). When a cell divides by way of meiosis, it produces four cells, called gametes (reproduction).

subjective.topic: E. Cell Cycle, Mitosis and Meiosis
subjective.question: Name the stages of prophase I of meiosis.
subjective.answer: Prophase I occupies more than 90% of the time required for meiosis. Its sub-stages are: (1) Leptotene, (2) Zygotene, (3) Pachytene, (4) Diplotene, (5) Diakinesis.

subjective.topic: E. Cell Cycle, Mitosis and Meiosis
subjective.question: Describe prophase II of meiosis.
subjective.answer: Meiosis II begins without any further replication of the chromosomes. In prophase II, no replication of chromosomes occurs as they are already replicated; centrioles are separated and take positions on the opposite poles of the cell; the nuclear membrane/envelope disappears and breaks down; and spindle fibres form and radiate toward the centre of the cell, forming the spindle apparatus.

subjective.topic: E. Cell Cycle, Mitosis and Meiosis
subjective.question: What do you know about telophase II of meiosis?
subjective.answer: In telophase II, the chromosomes arrive at opposite poles, the nuclear membrane forms and the chromosomes begin de-condensing. Cytokinesis occurs. The two cells produced by meiosis I divide to form four haploid daughter cells, each with a haploid set of chromosomes and genetically distinct from the others and from the parent cell. When telophase II is over, the cells are entirely separated and their nuclear membranes are fully formed; meiosis is then complete.

subjective.topic: E. Cell Cycle, Mitosis and Meiosis
subjective.question: Differentiate between telophase I and telophase II.
subjective.answer: The difference between telophase I in meiosis and telophase in mitosis is that, located close to each pole of the spindle, is a haploid set of chromosomes. Limited uncoiling occurs before the chromosomes move onto the second cell division stage in meiosis, telophase II.

subjective.topic: E. Cell Cycle, Mitosis and Meiosis
subjective.question: Define spermatogenesis and oogenesis. What is the difference between them?
subjective.answer: Meiosis in males is called spermatogenesis and produces sperms; meiosis in females is called oogenesis and produces ova. Spermatogenesis: four sperm cells are produced from a primary spermatocyte. Oogenesis: only one ovum (egg) is produced from each primary oocyte, and the polar bodies die. Meiosis, the process by which gametes are formed, can also be called gametogenesis.

subjective.topic: E. Cell Cycle, Mitosis and Meiosis
subjective.question: Which type of cell division is present in somatic cells?
subjective.answer: Mitosis. Somatic (body) cells divide by mitosis, producing two diploid daughter cells identical to the parent cell.

subjective.topic: E. Cell Cycle, Mitosis and Meiosis
subjective.question: Write the Frederick Griffith experiment.
subjective.answer: Griffith's experiments: the first clue that DNA was the carrier of hereditary information came from the work of Fred Griffith in 1928. He observed the phenomenon of transformation in the bacterium Streptococcus pneumoniae. Griffith had isolated different strains of S. pneumoniae: in the virulent strain, each bacterium is surrounded by a polysaccharide coat, which makes the bacterial colony appear smooth on an agar plate (S forms). These virulent forms occasionally get mutated to non-virulent forms, which lack a polysaccharide coat and produce rough-appearing colonies (R forms). Griffith carried out a series of transformation experiments using S-form and R-form strains of S. pneumoniae and mice as the experimental animal.

subjective.question: Write the experiment of T. H. Morgan.
subjective.answer: Eye colour trait is linked with the sex of Drosophila; Morgan with an experiment proved that the eye colour trait is linked with the sex of the drosophila. Experiment: male flies were with white eyes (mutant); female flies were with red eyes (wild type). Progeny F1 was with red eyes - all the flies produced during the F1 generation were with red eyes. Progeny F2 showed a 3:1 ratio (three red eye : one white eye); the white-eyed trait appeared only in males - all females and half the males had red eyes. Morgan's discovery: transmission of the X chromosome correlates with inheritance of the eye colour trait - the first solid evidence indicating that a gene is associated with a specific chromosome.

subjective.question: What is linkage mapping?
subjective.answer: Linkage mapping is critical for identifying the location of genes that cause genetic diseases.

subjective.question: Define linkage map.
subjective.answer: A linkage map is a genetic map of a species that shows the position of its known genes or genetic markers relative to each other in terms of recombination frequency.

subjective.question: Define genetic mapping in humans.
subjective.answer: Genetic mapping, also called linkage mapping, provides clues about which chromosome contains the gene and precisely where it lies on that chromosome.

subjective.question: How is genetic mapping performed?
subjective.answer: Scientists isolate DNA from samples and examine it for the unique patterns of bases. Molecular techniques are referred to as genotyping polymorphisms or markers.

subjective.question: What is the method of mapping gene disorders?
subjective.answer: Genetic maps have been used successfully to find the single gene responsible for inherited disorders, like cystic fibrosis and muscular dystrophy.

subjective.question: What is recombination frequency?
subjective.answer: Recombination frequency is the frequency of recombinant offspring; it reflects the distances between genes on chromosomes.

subjective.question: What is a map unit (centimorgan)? How is a genetic map related to recombination frequency?
subjective.answer: A genetic map is a map based on the frequencies of recombination between markers during crossover of homologous chromosomes. Sturtevant expressed the distance between genes as map units: one map unit (1 cM, centimorgan) is equivalent to a 1% recombination frequency.

subjective.question: Write the names of markers used in linkage mapping.
subjective.answer: Markers used in mapping/linkage maps are: microsatellites and restriction fragment length polymorphisms (RFLPs).

subjective.question: What are the types of genetic markers?
subjective.answer: There are several different types of genetic markers; the types most used on genetic maps are microsatellites and SNPs.

subjective.question: Write the applications of molecular markers.
subjective.answer: Short-range applications: parentage determination, genetic distance estimation and determination of twin zygosity. Long-range applications: gene mapping and mapping of QTL by linkage, and marker-assisted selection of breeds.

subjective.question: Name the genes used in gene mapping of Drosophila and write their recombination frequencies.
subjective.answer: In Drosophila gene mapping, the genes used include cn, b and vg. Recombination frequency between cn and b is 9%; between cn and vg is 9.5%; and recombination frequency between b and vg is 17%. (A linkage map shows the position of known genes or genetic markers relative to each other in terms of recombination frequency.)

subjective.question: What is the effect of linkage on inheritance?
subjective.answer: Morgan did another experiment with fruit flies to see how linkage affects the inheritance of two different characters: body colour (wild type grey, mutant black) and wing size (wild type normal, mutant vestigial). According to independent assortment, four phenotypes in a 1:1:1:1 ratio were expected; instead, a large number of wild-type and double-mutant flies were observed, showing that the genes are linked and do not assort independently (results due to linkage and crossing over).

subjective.question: What is positional cloning?
subjective.answer: Positional cloning is a laboratory technique used to locate the position of a disease-associated gene along the chromosome. This approach works even when little or no information is available about the biochemical basis of the disease. Positional cloning is used in conjunction with linkage analysis.

subjective.question: What is a unit map?
subjective.answer: RFLPs are used for constructing genetic maps: RFLPs can be used to measure recombination rates, which can lead to a genetic map with the distance between RFLP loci (expressed in map units).

subjective.question: What is the SRY gene and what is its importance?
subjective.answer: Researchers have found the SRY gene (sex-determining region of the Y chromosome). The SRY protein is the testis-determining factor (TDF); this gene is responsible for the initiation of male sex determination in humans. In individuals with the SRY gene, the generic embryonic gonads are modified into testes; the SRY protein is a transcription factor, which attaches (binds) to specific regions of DNA and helps control the activity of particular genes. In addition, other genes on the Y chromosome are necessary for the production of functional sperms. In individuals lacking the SRY gene, the generic embryonic gonads develop into ovaries.

subjective.question: What are sex-linked traits and disorders? Name human sex-linked disorders.
subjective.answer: Genes on the X or Y chromosome are called sex-linked. For example, an X-linked recessive allele in humans causes haemophilia, which is much more common in males than females because males express the trait when they inherit one mutant allele. Human sex-linked disorders include: colour blindness, Duchenne muscular dystrophy and haemophilia. X-linked recessive disorders listed in the sources: Duchenne muscular dystrophy, Hunter's disease, Menkes disease, haemophilia A and B, and colour blindness.

subjective.question: Define mutation.
subjective.answer: Mutation indicates "a change", while in other disciplines it is used to indicate "a disease-causing change". Mutations may be harmful, beneficial, or may have no effect.

subjective.question: What is a point mutation? Write its cause/effect.
subjective.answer: A point mutation or substitution is a genetic mutation where a single nucleotide base is changed, inserted or deleted from a sequence of DNA or RNA; point mutations affect single sites on DNA - substitution of one base for another. Point mutations have a variety of effects on the downstream protein product. Cause/effect: the protein may lose its function, which can result in a disease in the organism. For example, sickle cell disease is caused by a single point mutation (a missense mutation) in the beta-haemoglobin gene that converts a GAG codon into GUG, which encodes the amino acid valine rather than glutamic acid.

subjective.question: Which mutation produces a change in the amino acid in the protein product?
subjective.answer: A missense mutation. It is a type of point mutation in which a single nucleotide change results in a codon that codes for a different amino acid, so the amino acid sequence of the protein product is changed (e.g. the GAG to GUG change in the beta-haemoglobin gene in sickle cell disease, where glutamic acid is replaced by valine).

subjective.question: What is a frameshift mutation?
subjective.answer: A frameshift mutation is caused by the insertion or deletion of a number of nucleotides in a DNA sequence that is not divisible by three. Because codons are read in triplets, the reading frame of the gene shifts from the point of mutation, so all the amino acids after that point are changed and the resulting protein is usually non-functional.

subjective.question: Differentiate between forward, reverse and neutral mutations.
subjective.answer: Forward mutation: a mutation that changes the wild-type (normal) phenotype into a mutant phenotype. Reverse mutation (reversion): a second mutation that restores the wild-type phenotype, either by exactly reversing the original change or by a suppressor change elsewhere. Neutral mutation: a mutation that has no detectable effect on the phenotype or fitness of the organism - it neither harms nor benefits it.

subjective.question: How do mutant alleles alter gene function?
subjective.answer: A mutant allele can alter gene function in several ways: it may cause loss of function (the gene product is absent or non-functional, e.g. a null or missense change that inactivates the protein), gain of function (the product becomes overactive or gains a new activity), or a change in the amount of product (mutations in regulatory regions altering expression). The altered protein may lose its normal function, which can result in a disease in the organism - for example, the single point mutation in the beta-haemoglobin gene produces abnormal haemoglobin in sickle cell disease.

subjective.question: What is an inversion mutation and what are its effects?
subjective.answer: In an inversion mutation, a segment of the gene/chromosome is reversed end to end; inversion mutations only affect a small part of the gene. Example from the sources: normal gene sequence GGTCTCCTCACGCCA (codons giving Pro-Glu-Glu-Cys-Gly) becomes GGTCCTCTCACGCCA after inversion (giving Pro-Gly-Glu-Cys-Gly) - i.e. the order of bases changes and the amino acid sequence of the protein is altered at that position.

subjective.question: Write the rules for mutation nomenclature.
subjective.answer: All variants should be described at the most basic level, i.e. DNA level. Descriptions should always be in relation to a reference sequence, either a genomic or a coding DNA sequence; in practice a coding DNA reference sequence is preferred (good for promoters, alternative splicing etc.). To avoid confusion, the description of a variant should be preceded by a letter indicating the type of reference sequence used: "c." for a coding DNA sequence (e.g. c.76A>T), "g." for a genomic sequence (e.g. g.476A>T), "m." for a mitochondrial sequence (e.g. m.8993T>C), "r." for an RNA sequence (e.g. r.76a>u), and "p." for a protein sequence (e.g. p.Lys76Asn). For describing genes/proteins, only official HGNC (HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee) gene symbols should be used.

subjective.question: What are structural abnormalities of chromosomes?
subjective.answer: Structural abnormalities are when part of an individual chromosome is missing, extra, switched to another chromosome, or turned upside down. Any alteration, addition or deletion of a chromosomal part leads to alteration of the number, position or sequence of genes in the chromosome. Types based on genetic material: (1) Balanced - the chromosome complement is complete. (2) Unbalanced - there is an incorrect amount of genetic material. Deletions are one type: for point deletions, one nucleotide has been deleted from the sequence (associated with cystic fibrosis, Turner syndrome; results in frameshift mutation).

subjective.question: What types of deletion are there?
subjective.answer: Terminal deletion: a deletion that occurs towards the end of a chromosome. Intercalary/interstitial deletion: a deletion that occurs from the interior of a chromosome.

subjective.question: What is microdeletion?
subjective.answer: A microdeletion is a relatively small amount of deletion (up to 5 Mb) that could include a dozen genes.

subjective.question: What is a suppressor mutation? Differentiate between intragenic and intergenic suppression.
subjective.answer: A suppressor mutation suppresses the effect of another mutation and occurs at a site different from the site of the original mutation. Intragenic suppression results from suppressor mutations that occur in the same gene as the original mutation. Intergenic (extragenic) suppression relieves the effects of a mutation in one gene by a mutation somewhere else within the genome; the second mutation is not on the same gene as the original mutation.

subjective.question: What is aneuploidy?
subjective.answer: Aneuploidy is the variation/change in chromosome number that can occur by the addition or deletion of a chromosome or part of a chromosome (an abnormal number of chromosomes in a cell, e.g. trisomy and monosomy).

subjective.question: What is euploidy?
subjective.answer: Euploidy is the gain of one or more complete sets of chromosomes (a chromosome number that is an exact multiple of the haploid set).

subjective.question: What is polyploidy? Write its types.
subjective.answer: Polyploidy is the heritable condition of possessing more than two complete sets of chromosomes. Two major types of polyploidy: (1) Autopolyploidy, (2) Allopolyploidy.

subjective.question: What is trisomy?
subjective.answer: Trisomy is a type of polysomy in which there are three copies of a particular chromosome instead of the normal two. Trisomy is a type of aneuploidy. Trisomy of chromosome 21, which is found in Down syndrome, is called trisomy 21.

subjective.question: What is monosomy? Write its causes.
subjective.answer: Monosomy is the state of having a single copy of a chromosome pair instead of the usual two copies found in diploid cells. Causes of monosomy: (1) Non-disjunction - one gamete receives two copies of homologous chromosomes and the other will have no copy. (2) Loss of a chromosome as it moves towards the pole of the cell during anaphase. Monosomy is the cause of some human diseases such as Turner syndrome and Cri du chat syndrome.

subjective.question: What is a genetic disorder?
subjective.answer: A genetic disorder is a genetic problem caused by one or more abnormalities in the genome. Most genetic disorders are quite rare and affect one person in every several thousands or millions. Genetic disorders may be hereditary, meaning that they are passed down from the parents' genes.

subjective.question: Explain sickle cell anaemia.
subjective.answer: Sickle cell anaemia (sickle cell disease) is a disorder of the blood caused by an inherited abnormal haemoglobin (the oxygen-carrying protein within the red blood cells). The abnormal haemoglobin causes distorted (sickled) red blood cells. The sickled red blood cells are fragile and prone to rupture. It is an inherited red blood cell disorder in which there are not enough healthy red blood cells to carry oxygen throughout the body; normally, the flexible, round red blood cells move easily through blood vessels.

subjective.question: What are autosomal dominant disorders? Write their frequency.
subjective.answer: A single abnormal gene on one of the first 22 non-sex (autosomal) chromosomes from either parent can cause an autosomal disorder; dominant inheritance means an abnormal gene from one parent can cause disease. Examples of autosomal dominant disorders include Marfan syndrome and neurofibromatosis type 1. The frequency of autosomal dominant disorders varies between 3 - 9.5 per 1000 individuals.

subjective.question: Write the frequency of autosomal recessive disorders.
subjective.answer: The frequency of autosomal recessive disorders is between 2 - 2.5 per 1000 individuals.

subjective.question: Write down at least three mitochondrial diseases.
subjective.answer: Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes (MELAS); Kearns-Sayre syndrome; and NARP - NARP stands for neurogenic weakness, ataxia and retinitis pigmentosa.

subjective.question: Differentiate between single-gene and multifactorial disorders.
subjective.answer: Single-gene disorders are caused by DNA changes in one particular gene and often have predictable inheritance patterns; over 10,000 human disorders are caused by a change (mutation) in a single gene. Conditions caused by many contributing factors (many genes plus environment) are called complex or multifactorial disorders; researchers are learning that nearly all conditions and diseases have a genetic component.

subjective.question: Write down the six diseases of multifactorial diseases.
subjective.answer: Genetic disorders controlled by many genes plus the effects of the environment - six multifactorial diseases: (1) Asthma, (2) Cancers, (3) Diabetes, (4) Heart diseases, (5) Hypertension, (6) Obesity.

subjective.question: Write the diagnostic tests for genetic disorders.
subjective.answer: Physical analysis: physical analysis of the affected individual. Ultrasonography of the fetus: determines malformations of head, internal organs and extremities. Analysis of amniotic fluids: amniotic fluid analysis to determine genetic and chromosomal disorders after 14 weeks of gestation; more than 200 various genetic diseases can easily be detected. Maternal blood analysis: maternal blood analysis to observe an abnormal fetus.

subjective.question: What is genomic imprinting?
subjective.answer: Genomic imprinting is the epigenetic marking of a locus on the basis of parental origin. It results in monoallelic gene expression: some genes are expressed only from the maternal genome and some only from the paternal genome. It is estimated that about 40 genes are imprinted and they can be found on several different chromosomes.

subjective.question: Define polymorphism.
subjective.answer: Polymorphism, in biology, is a discontinuous genetic variation resulting in the occurrence of several different forms or types of individuals among the members of a single species.

subjective.question: What is the role of cisplatin in cancer treatment?
subjective.answer: Cisplatin is a chemotherapy medication used to treat a number of cancers. This includes testicular cancer, ovarian cancer, cervical cancer, breast cancer, bladder cancer, head and neck cancer and oesophageal cancer.

subjective.question: Write the principle of PCR and its steps.
subjective.answer: PCR stands for polymerase chain reaction. It is a widely used technique of DNA amplification, given by Kary Mullis. Principle: this technique amplifies a gene in vitro to produce billions of copies of a particular DNA in a short time. Steps: Step 1 - Denaturation: the solution contained in the tube is heated to at least 94 degrees C using a thermal cycler. Step 2 - Annealing. Step 3 - Extension. Step 4 - Analysis with electrophoresis.

subjective.question: What is the role of MgCl2 in PCR and of EDTA in gel electrophoresis buffer?
subjective.answer: In PCR, MgCl2 is an essential cofactor that enhances the activity of Taq DNA polymerase, which in turn increases the amplification rate of DNA; however, higher concentrations of MgCl2 can result in decreased specificity. In agarose gel electrophoresis, EDTA is added in the buffer for chelating the magnesium ions which are cofactors for DNA nucleases; hence the activity of DNA nucleases that may be present is inhibited, and DNA is protected from degradation by DNA nucleases.

subjective.question: What is the electroporation technique?
subjective.answer: Electroporation, or electropermeabilization, is a microbiology technique in which an electrical field is applied to cells in order to increase the permeability of the cell membrane, allowing chemicals, drugs or DNA to be introduced into the cell. In microbiology, electroporation is often used to transform bacteria, yeast or plant protoplasts by introducing new coding DNA: if bacteria and plasmids are mixed together, the plasmids can be transferred into the bacteria after electroporation. Electroporation works by passing thousands of volts across a distance of one to two millimetres of suspended cells in an electroporation cuvette (1.0-1.5 kV, 250-750 V/cm). Afterwards, the cells have to be handled carefully until they have had a chance to divide, producing new cells that contain reproduced plasmids. This process is approximately ten times more effective than chemical transformation.

subjective.question: How is a plasmid used as a cloning vector with high and low molecular weight?
subjective.answer: Conjugative plasmids: high molecular weight and have one to three copies per cell. Non-conjugative plasmids: low molecular weight and have multiple copies per cell. Host range is determined by the ori region; it can be either broad host range or restricted host range - Col E1 has a restricted host range, while promiscuous plasmids have a broad host range.

subjective.question: What are natural plasmids?
subjective.answer: Plasmids found in nature often give their hosts beneficial traits that allow them to survive in competitive environments. Plasmids derived directly from the environment are sometimes called "natural plasmids", to distinguish them from the modified versions we usually work with in the lab.

subjective.question: How do plasmids play an important role in microbial resistance against antibiotics?
subjective.answer: Plasmids can transfer between different bacteria. This means that a bacterium can become resistant to multiple antibiotics at once by picking up a single plasmid; they then become multidrug-resistant. Furthermore, genes that influence bacterial virulence are also frequently found on plasmids.

subjective.question: What is the western blotting technique used for?
subjective.answer: The western blot (sometimes called the protein immunoblot) is a widely used analytical technique in molecular biology, immunogenetics and other molecular biology disciplines to detect specific proteins in a sample of tissue homogenate or extract.

subjective.question: Define autoradiography.
subjective.answer: An autoradiograph is an image on an X-ray film or nuclear emulsion produced by the pattern of decay emissions (e.g. beta particles or gamma rays) from a distribution of a radioactive substance. The film or emulsion is apposed to the labelled tissue section to obtain the autoradiograph (also called an autoradiogram).

subjective.question: Define proteomics.
subjective.answer: Proteomics is the study of proteomes and their functions.

subjective.question: Define palindromic sequence.
subjective.answer: A palindromic sequence is a nucleic acid sequence on double-stranded DNA or RNA wherein reading 5' to 3' forward on one strand matches the sequence reading 5' to 3' on the complementary strand with which it forms a double helix. A palindromic nucleotide sequence can form a hairpin.

subjective.question: Define isopycnic centrifugation.
subjective.answer: Isopycnic means of, relating to, or marked by equal or constant density. Isopycnic centrifugation is a technique in which the components of a mixture are separated on the basis of differences in density.

subjective.question: What are the primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structures of a protein?
subjective.answer: The different levels of protein structure are known as primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure. The primary structure is the sequence of amino acids that make up a polypeptide chain; the exact order of the amino acids in a specific protein is the primary sequence for that protein.

subjective.question: What are the domains of a protein?
subjective.answer: A protein domain is a conserved part of a given protein sequence and (tertiary) structure that can evolve, function and exist independently of the rest of the protein chain. Each domain forms a compact three-dimensional structure and often can be independently stable and folded.

subjective.question: What was the ancient pregnancy test?
subjective.answer: In the first known pregnancy tests, ancient Egyptian women urinated on barley or wheat seeds: quickly sprouting seeds indicated pregnancy. While this may sound like pseudoscience, several modern studies have shown that it works pretty well, correctly identifying 70-85% of pregnancies.

subjective.question: What is green technology? Give one example.
subjective.answer: One of the best known examples of green technology is the solar cell. A solar cell directly converts the energy in light into electrical energy through the process of photovoltaics. Generating electricity from solar energy means less consumption of fossil fuels, reducing pollution and greenhouse gas emissions.

subjective.question: What is the human genome and the bacterial genome?
subjective.answer: Human genome: all the genetic information in a person; the human genome is made up of the DNA in chromosomes as well as the DNA in mitochondria. Most bacteria have a genome that consists of a single DNA molecule (i.e. one chromosome) that is several million base pairs in size and is "circular" (does not have ends like the chromosomes of eukaryotic organisms).

subjective.question: What is the size of a human gene?
subjective.answer: Genes range in size from 994 to 41.8 kb for mouse (average length = 7902 bp) and from 1148 to 37.7 kb for human (average length = 8446 bp). The number of exons ranges from 1 to 41 per gene (average 8.4).

subjective.question: What is sub-genetic information?
subjective.answer: Sub-genetic information is the material inside the nucleus of cells that carries genetic information. Example of lay language for DNA: "The genetic material inside your cells" - encoded in the genes, DNA is used to make protein and RNA molecules.

subjective.question: What is VNTR? Write the applications of VNTR.
subjective.answer: VNTRs (variable number tandem repeats) are short nucleotide sequences organized as a tandem repeat on genomes; they are found on many chromosomes and show variations in length between individuals. Applications of VNTR: microbiology, DNA fingerprinting, genetic diversity, forensics, mapping of genomes, and breeding patterns of wild or domesticated animals.

subjective.question: What is the function of STR?
subjective.answer: Short tandem repeat (STR) analysis is one of the most useful methods in molecular biology, used to compare specific loci on DNA from two or more samples. A short tandem repeat is a microsatellite consisting of a unit of two to thirteen nucleotides repeated hundreds of times in a row on the DNA strand.

subjective.question: During DNA extraction, how are proteins denatured?
subjective.answer: By adding proteinase.

subjective.question: Name some factors which help in the mobility of DNA.
subjective.answer: In gel electrophoresis, the mobility of DNA depends on: (1) the size/length of the DNA fragment - smaller fragments move faster and farther; (2) the negative charge on DNA, which makes it migrate toward the positive electrode; (3) the concentration of the agarose gel - higher concentration slows migration; (4) the voltage applied; and (5) the composition of the running buffer. (This question appears in the solved past-paper file without a printed answer.)

subjective.question: Differentiate between forward and reverse genetics.
subjective.answer: Reverse genetics is a method used to help understand the function of a gene by analyzing the phenotypic effects of specific engineered gene sequences. Reverse genetics usually proceeds in the opposite direction of so-called forward genetic screens of classical genetics (in forward genetics, one starts from a phenotype/mutant and finds the responsible gene; in reverse genetics, one starts from a known gene sequence and studies the resulting phenotype).

subjective.topic: A. Mendelian Genetics and Basic Concepts
subjective.question: Define genetics.
subjective.answer: Genetics is the branch of biology that deals with heredity and variation. It is the study of genes, how characteristics (traits) are transmitted from parents to offspring, and how genes are structured, expressed and regulated.

subjective.question: What is epigenetics?
subjective.answer: Epigenetics is the study of heritable changes in gene function or expression that do not involve any change in the DNA sequence itself. These changes occur through chemical modifications such as DNA methylation and histone modification, which switch genes on or off, and they can be influenced by environmental factors.

subjective.question: Describe the causes (mechanisms and factors) of epigenetics.
subjective.answer: The primary molecular mechanisms of epigenetics are: (1) DNA methylation - addition of a methyl group to the cytosine base of DNA, which usually silences the gene; and (2) histone modification - chemical changes (such as acetylation and methylation) of histone proteins that open or close the chromatin. Non-coding RNAs also play a role. The epigenome is affected by environmental factors such as diet, exposure to toxins, stress hormones, the nutrition of the mother during pregnancy, social interactions and physical activity.

subjective.question: What are the causes of variation?
subjective.answer: Causes of variation are of two kinds. Genetic causes: meiosis (crossing over and independent assortment), sexual reproduction (new combinations of genes) and mutations. Environmental causes: nutrients, drugs, temperature and physical training. Many variations result from a combination of genetic makeup and environment.

subjective.question: Name the types of epistasis and briefly describe them.
subjective.answer: There are six common types of epistasis gene interactions: (1) Dominant epistasis - a dominant allele at one locus masks the expression of alleles at another locus, e.g. fruit color in summer squash. (2) Recessive epistasis - the homozygous recessive condition at one locus masks the other locus, e.g. coat color in mice and Labrador retriever. (3) Dominant inhibitory epistasis - a dominant allele at one locus inhibits the expression of another gene. (4) Duplicate dominant epistasis - a dominant allele at either of two loci produces the same phenotype, e.g. capsule shape in shepherd's purse. (5) Duplicate recessive epistasis - recessive alleles at either locus produce the same phenotype. (6) Polymeric gene interaction - two genes interact additively to produce a trait, e.g. fruit shape in summer squash types.

subjective.question: Write a note on the size of chromosomes during different stages of mitosis.
subjective.answer: There is variation in the size of chromosomes during the different stages of mitosis. In interphase the chromosomes are longest and thinnest. During prophase there is a progressive decrease in their length accompanied by an increase in thickness. In anaphase the chromosomes are smallest. Chromosomes can be easily observed and are generally measured during metaphase, so chromosomes are studied at mitotic metaphase.

subjective.question: What is the function of SNP?
subjective.answer: SNP (single nucleotide polymorphism) is a variation of a single nucleotide at a specific position in the DNA sequence, found in both coding and non-coding regions. SNPs are the most common genetic markers; they are used in genetic (linkage) mapping, in identifying disease-causing genes and disease associations, in forensic studies and in population genetics. Non-synonymous SNPs change the amino acid sequence and can alter protein function.

subjective.question: What is AFLP?
subjective.answer: AFLP (Amplified Fragment Length Polymorphism) is a molecular marker technique in which DNA is cut with restriction enzymes and selected fragments are amplified by PCR to produce a fingerprint pattern of DNA fragments. It is used for DNA fingerprinting, genetic mapping, and the study of genetic diversity and relatedness among organisms.

subjective.question: Write a note on color blindness and its pattern of inheritance.
subjective.answer: Color blindness (color deficiency) is an X-linked recessive disorder in which a person is unable to see colors in a normal way and cannot distinguish between certain colors, usually greens and reds, and occasionally blues. A normal female is XX and a normal male is XY; a color-blind female is XcXc, a carrier female is XcX and a color-blind male is XcY. A color-blind mother transmits the mutant allele to all of her sons, while a carrier mother transmits it to 50% of her sons.

subjective.question: Define non-disjunction.
subjective.answer: Non-disjunction is the failure of homologous chromosomes (in meiosis I) or sister chromatids (in meiosis II) to separate properly during cell division. As a result, one gamete receives two copies of a homologous chromosome and the other gamete receives no copy. After fertilization this produces aneuploidy - trisomy (an extra chromosome) or monosomy (a missing chromosome). Loss of a chromosome as it moves towards the pole during anaphase can also cause monosomy.

subjective.question: What are fragile X chromosomes? Describe fragile X syndrome.
subjective.answer: Fragile X syndrome is a genetic disorder associated with a fragile site on the X chromosome. It is most commonly caused by a CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the 5' region of the FMR1 gene. Unaffected individuals have about 6-50 CGG repeats. In individuals with fragile X syndrome more than 200 CGG repeats are present, which is correlated with hypermethylation at CpG dinucleotides and silencing of the FMR1 gene, resulting in intellectual disability.
